narrative:
The model estimated a 96% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. In this admission process, that prediction is treated as a strong signal of academic risk, so your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven most by your third-year class standing. You were in the lowest decile, while accepted students averaged near the middle of their class; this was the single strongest factor and pushed the prediction toward bar failure. Your first-year standing was the second most influential factor: at decile 2 versus an accepted-student average of 6, it also pushed toward failure, though less strongly than your third-year record. Your LSAT score was the third most important factor; at 28 compared with an accepted average of about 37, it added further risk toward failure. These academic signals outweighed your middle-income background and full-time status.

To move forward, ask admissions whether any record was misread, especially class-rank data. Then build a concrete improvement plan: consult an academic advisor about raising your standing, consider structured LSAT preparation and a retake if feasible, and seek bar-exam readiness support. Reapply only after you can show stronger academic evidence, and consider schools or pathways that review applicants more holistically.
